newsitem.title: USA: Kansas attorney general hails sex predator ruling.
newsitem.headline: Kansas attorney general hails sex predator ruling.

text.p: A Supreme Court decision upholding a Kansas law allowing sex offenders to be confined to mental institutions after their release from jail was hailed Monday by the state attorney general, who said she hoped it would encourage other states to adopt such measures.

"It is such a victory for the states today to know that we can protect people that would otherwise be victims from sexual predation," Kansas Attorney General Carla Stovall said in a teleconference from Jackson Hole, Wyo., where she was attending a meeting of the National Association of Attorneys General.

The high court upheld by a 5-4 vote a Kansas law that provides for the civil commitment of mentally ill sex offenders who pose a great risk of committing more crimes involving children if released into the community.
The ruling was a legal boost for similar laws in Washington, Arizona, Wisconsin, Minnesota and California, and Stovall said the court's decision would likely spawn more states to adopt such laws.

"I truly believe that God today is taking care of the children in this country by letting us enact laws like this to protect from the worst kind of predators that there are -- the ones that just don't stop and won't stop until they get intensive, in-depth treatment," she said.

She said she was encouraged that Justice Clarence Thomas wrote for the court that the Kansas law did not violate constitutional due process or double jeopardy rights -- the protection against being tried twice for the same crime.

In Kansas, she said, the length of time an offender would be committed depended on the offender's progress during treatment. "It will absolutely be on a case-by-case evaluation, but experts say that about three to five years is the length of time that's needed for intensive treatment for pedophiles and sexual sadists."
Stovall conceded the court's ruling could clear the way for states to pass laws allowing for the civil commitment of people suffering from other mental ailments such as pyromania.

"This would open the door to states to civilly commit other kinds of wrongdoers," she said. "That possibility has been created that you could commit those individuals as long as you could show dangerousness as well."
An aide to Stovall said more than 800 convicted sex offenders in Kansas prisons would now be eligible for committal when their sentences end.
Stephen McAllister, a law professor at the University of Kansas who drafted all the state's legal briefs in the case, said he felt vindicated after learning of the court's ruling.

"In a lot of ways I think this is more humane and is certainly an important tool, at least for the state to be able to do it with people where there is some promise where it can help," McAllister said.

The Kansas case involved Leroy Hendricks, 62, a convicted child molester with a long record of sex crimes. Kansas sought to have him committed to a mental facility in anticipation of his release from prison after serving 10 years.

A jury found he was a violent sex predator likely to commit similar crimes if released and ordered his confinement to a state hospital for treatment. He became the first of a small group of sex offenders involuntarily committed under the law.
Attorneys for Hendricks were not immediately available to comment on the Supreme Court ruling.
